prop.family: My brother recorded the old station ident. On the outtake I'm called Mercury.
prop.clip: Your mic is still on, Mercury.

events.text: From the pay phone by the van, a stringer tells you: 'Mavis says the backup mast is purple.' No one else is on the call.
Rita's vermilion cassette tin belongs in the locked audition drawer. A lamp counts down to the wire weather handoff.
Inside the booth you see Phil put the missing cassette tin back in Rita's tray, seal intact.
The sealed tin is now in Rita's tray.
You see Phil lift the room loudspeaker plug before the archive splice passes the head. The public speaker stays silent.
The public speaker meter reads zero during the line test.
You woke in the hotel with the same date on the radio. At the station the drawer is locked again.
The vermilion tin is sealed inside the drawer. Only printed wire weather is released for air this morning. A red lamp shows eight seconds to the handoff.
Phil reads the printed wire weather on the live return.
The wire booking owns the rest of the slot.
Rita takes the master key off its hook. Phil is removed from the booth roster until the end of this shift.

decision.note: The tin is in my tray, seal intact. That's enough. I don't owe Phil a story about a name my brother whispered into a mic in a kitchen that no longer exists. I check the line meter, confirm the channel is clean, and let the lamp burn its last eighty seconds. The handoff is mine to shape. I will give this broadcast a voice that is not the wire's voice. Mercury stays in the drawer. The combination is 5066 and it stays 5066. I slide my thumb across the fader, listen to the room tone, and wait for my cue. Phil can have his weather card when the clock says so. Right now the meters are mine and the air is mine and that is the whole arrangement.

Thirty-five seconds, acoustic window clear, public speaker already dead. Phil pulled the plug on the room speaker right before the splice hit the head, so nothing leaked. The tin is in my tray, seal intact, the way it should be. I'm not sending it to the copy desk. That outtake — "Your mic is still on, Mercury" — is not a public record. It's my brother's tape, my name on it in a room where I didn't want a name. I lock 5066, I keep the key in my palm, and I decide later, on my schedule, how much of that ident the morning air hears. The distinctive broadcast I promised is the ident, clean, not the flinch after it. The archive belongs to me. It stays in my drawer.

Eight seconds. The red lamp is burning. The tin is sealed, the drawer is locked, and I locked it myself two wakes ago by pulling the speaker plug before the splice hit the head. Rita re-locked it. I re-sealed it. That's the pattern and I'm not the one to break it on a Tuesday morning with the same date still ticking off the radio. Pittsburgh needs a weather line, not a decision from me about whether Rita's cassette tin gets to speak. So I take the printed wire, read it clean, get the routine sign-off, and let my name sit on a perfectly ordinary forecast. The tin stays in the drawer. The lamp hits zero. The wire goes out. That's the job this morning and I will not make it anything more.

The wire is safe and sound, but it isn't ours. The ident my brother cut is in that drawer behind the combination, and the vermilion tin is sealed up there with it. Eight seconds on the red lamp, Phil already on the live return reading the same grey copy every station reads. If I let the roster stand and walk away from the key, whatever is in that tin gets handled by someone who'll log it as 'misc. archive' and play it under a network tag. The archive is mine. I pocket the key, tell Phil the booth is closed for the rest of the shift, and I'll pull the ident myself when the clock hits zero. 'Your mic is still on, Mercury.' Let them hear it the way it was meant to be heard.
